data: Forecasting market volatility, and what it is actually worth to an investor

A nine-phase research project. Walk-forward models forecast next-day S&P 500 volatility well. Better forecasts did not raise return per unit of risk, but they reliably cut losses in crashes. Diversifying across stocks, bonds and gold did more for risk-adjusted return than any forecast. Safeguards: walk-forward fitting, one-day execution delay, trading costs, bootstrap confidence intervals, a Sharpe ratio deflated for the number of strategies tried, and a final test whose rules were committed before its data was downloaded.
Next-day volatility is predictable, and each added input helped.
HAR-RV, then VIX, a Fed-decision flag and the VIX term-structure slope; every step significant (Diebold-Mariano, p < 0.01); the slope model also won on a 2016+ holdout.
Past a basic model, better forecasts did not make a better portfolio.
Volatility-managed SPY beat buy & hold on Sharpe with every HAR model, but the most accurate model gave the lowest of the three, and every difference is inside its 95% bootstrap interval.
Protection has a price, and diversification is the cheapest source.
Equal weight SPY/IEF/GLD, rebalanced on a 5-point band, 2007-2026 with costs. The edge over SPY came mostly from 2007-2012.
Sharpe 0.75 vs 0.54; max drawdown -21% vs -55%; return 8.5% vs 10.7% a year
Out of sample, the volatility rule cut drawdowns everywhere but did not raise Sharpe.
Pre-registered test on 14 international country funds (rules committed before the data was downloaded).
Drawdown smaller in 14 of 14; Sharpe change -0.023 (95%: -0.131 to +0.085)

For an investor who wants a smoother ride, the evidence supports a diversified core (equal-weight stocks, bonds and gold) with optional volatility scaling, priced at roughly 0.9 points of return a year for about a third smaller crashes (average 2008-09 drawdown -61% to -43% across 14 countries). It does not support a claim of beating the market. This is research on historical data, not investment advice.

Tradable stand-ins: VXX (long volatility) and SVXY (short volatility). A walk-forward logistic regression on the gap between VIX and our forecast, VIX vs its 1-year mean, VIX momentum, the VIX/VIX3M term structure and the FOMC flag gives P(volatility rises). Sizing fixed in advance: full size at 65%+ confidence, half size at 55-65%, flat below. 5 bps costs, one-day execution delay.
Were the stated confidences honest? (10 years)

Reading it: the model was almost always short volatility, and its stated confidence was roughly honest. It still lost badly to simply holding SPY over 10 years, and the February 2018 volatility spike dominates. VXX only exists from 2018 (earlier days use 2x UVXY returns) and SVXY changed from -1x to -0.5x in 2018, so these numbers mix regimes. Verdict: rejected.
Parkinson range estimator RV = (ln(High/Low))^2 / (4 ln 2): uses the whole day's range, far less noisy than a squared close-to-close return.
Expanding window (1,000 days for the S&P index, 500 for ETFs), refit every 21 days. A forecast made at day t never uses data after day t.
Automated tests change future prices, VIX values and FOMC dates and confirm earlier forecasts and weights do not move (58 tests in total).
QLIKE (standard loss for variance forecasts) and MSE; Diebold-Mariano tests with Newey-West standard errors.
Orders execute one trading day after the signal (lag 1) in every headline result.
2 bps per unit of turnover for SPY/IEF, 3 bps GLD, 5-10 bps volatility products and country funds; cash earns T-bills, borrowing costs T-bills + 0.5%; weights drift between rebalances (Phase 8+).
95% moving-block bootstrap intervals (20-day blocks, 2,000 draws) on every Sharpe difference; Phase 9 resamples the same dates for every fund.
Deflated Sharpe ratio (Bailey and Lopez de Prado 2014) against the ~20 strategy variants tried, and against a conservative 50.
Phase 9's rules were committed to git (1e353f7) before its data was downloaded; results in a separate commit (1187584).
Intraday data is not used; Parkinson ignores overnight gaps.
20-25 years with a handful of crises; 20 years cannot confirm a 0.2 Sharpe advantage.
Training windows, refit interval, HAR windows and the 1e-8 floor were fixed in advance but other choices could change numbers.
Models are nested and several tests are not adjusted for multiple testing.
Simplified costs and borrowing; Phases 7-8 rely on a period when bonds mostly hedged stocks (until 2022) and gold rallied after 2024.
About 20 variants; the deflated Sharpe and Phase 9 address this, but the 2025+ final check is under two years long.
